summary: Specifies how a mobile node can move between networks and keep its IP address, with a home agent forwarding its traffic to wherever it currently is. This lets connections keep working as a device roams. It was replaced by RFC 3220.

eli5.summary: When you move house, the post office forwards your mail to the new place. Mobile IP forwards your internet packets to wherever you are now.

questions: how can a device keep its ip address while moving
how does mobile ip registration work
subtitle: How a laptop or phone can move between networks and keep the same IP address, with a home agent forwarding its traffic.

tldr.problem: IPv4 assumes an address identifies where a node is attached. A node that moves must either change its address, which breaks its connections, or have host-specific routes spread through the Internet, which does not scale.
tldr.mechanism: A mobile node keeps a fixed home address and registers a care-of address with its home agent. The home agent intercepts datagrams for the home address and tunnels them to the care-of address.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2002 was obsoleted by RFC 3220 and updated by RFC 2290, so it is no longer the current definition of IPv4 mobility support.

today: RFC 2002 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 3220 and was updated by RFC 2290. Use RFC 3220 for the later definition of IPv4 mobility support.

sections.title: The Mobility Problem and Its Cast
sections.content:
IP version 4 assumes that a node's IP address says where the node is attached. To move without losing its ability to communicate, a node would have to change its address, which makes it impossible to keep transport and higher-layer connections alive, or host-specific routes would have to spread through much of the Internet routing fabric, which has severe scaling problems. Mobile IP lets a node change its point of attachment without changing its IP address.

It adds three functional entities. A mobile node is a host or router that moves between networks. A home agent is a router on the mobile node's home network that tunnels datagrams to the node while it is away and keeps its current location. A foreign agent is a router on the visited network that provides routing services while the node is registered and removes the tunnel wrapping for delivery.

The mobile node keeps a long-term home address. Away from home it also has a care-of address, the end of the tunnel. This is either a foreign agent care-of address, which is preferred because many nodes can share it and it saves IPv4 addresses, or a co-located care-of address that the node obtains itself, for example through DHCP, and decapsulates on its own.

The RFC requires that a mobile node can talk to nodes with no mobility support, and that all messages updating a node's location are authenticated. It assumes a node does not change attachment more often than once per second, and it treats Mobile IP as a solution to "macro" mobility between subnets rather than fast handoff between nearby radio transceivers.
sections.eli5: You keep one permanent mailing address at your old house. Your parents there pass anything addressed to you on to wherever you are staying this week.

sections.title: Agent Discovery
sections.content:
Mobile IP uses ICMP Router Discovery to find agents. An Agent Advertisement is an ICMP Router Advertisement with a Mobility Agent Advertisement Extension (type 16) attached. It is sent with TTL 1 to 224.0.0.1 or 255.255.255.255. An Agent Solicitation is an ICMP Router Solicitation whose TTL MUST be 1.

The extension carries a sequence number, a registration lifetime, any care-of addresses, and flag bits: R (registration required), B (busy), H (home agent), F (foreign agent), M (minimal encapsulation), G (GRE encapsulation) and V (Van Jacobson header compression). Every advertisement MUST have at least one of F and H set. A Prefix-Lengths Extension (type 19) can say how many leading bits of each router address are the network number.

A mobile node detects a move in two ways. In the first, it records the ICMP lifetime of each advertisement and concludes it has lost an agent if it hears nothing from it before that lifetime ends. In the second, it compares network prefixes from the Prefix-Lengths Extension. If it hears from its own home agent, it has returned home and SHOULD deregister. Sequence numbers start at 0 after a reboot and run to 0xffff, which is followed by 256, so a node can tell a reboot from a rollover.

Solicitations are rate limited. A node MAY send three initial ones at one per second, then MUST back off exponentially, with a maximum interval that SHOULD be at least one minute.
sections.eli5: Helpers on each network shout "I can help visitors here!" every so often. A newcomer can also ask who is around, and tells whether it is home or away by whose voice it hears.

sections.title: Registration Messages
sections.content:
Registration is how a mobile node tells its home agent where it is, renews that, or deregisters when it returns home. It creates or changes a mobility binding at the home agent, which ties the home address to a care-of address for a lifetime. A node using a foreign agent care-of address MUST register through that foreign agent, which relays the request to the home agent and relays the reply back (four messages). Otherwise it registers directly with the home agent (two messages), though it SHOULD go through a foreign agent that sets the R bit.

Both messages travel in UDP to port 434. A Registration Request (type 1) has flag bits S (keep earlier bindings), B (forward broadcasts), D (the node decapsulates itself), M, G and V, followed by the lifetime, home address, home agent, care-of address and a 64-bit Identification. A lifetime of zero asks for deregistration and 0xffff means infinity. A Registration Reply (type 3) carries a result Code and the granted lifetime, which MAY be shorter than requested but never longer.

Reply codes are grouped. Codes 0 and 1 mean accepted, codes from 64 mean denied by the foreign agent (for example 67, mobile node failed authentication), and codes from 128 mean denied by the home agent (for example 133, registration Identification mismatch).

Every request and reply MUST contain exactly one Mobile-Home Authentication Extension (type 32). Optional extensions cover mobile-foreign (type 33) and foreign-home (type 34) authentication. The default authenticator is keyed MD5 in "prefix+suffix" mode, giving a 128-bit digest.
sections.eli5: When you reach your new place you call home and say "send my mail here, for this long". Your parents write back with yes or no, and a secret password proves the call is really you.

sections.title: Tunneling and Routing
sections.content:
Datagrams for the home address reach the home network by ordinary routing. The home agent intercepts them, wraps each in a tunnel to the care-of address, and the tunnel end hands the original to the mobile node. In the other direction, datagrams from the mobile node are generally delivered by standard IP routing and need not pass through the home agent.

Home agents and foreign agents MUST support IP in IP encapsulation. Minimal encapsulation and GRE are optional alternatives that the node can request with the M and G bits. A foreign agent that receives a tunneled datagram for a node not in its visitor list MUST NOT forward it unmodified, to avoid routing loops.

To intercept traffic on the home link, the home agent uses ARP tricks. While the node is away, the home agent answers ARP requests for the home address with proxy ARP, giving its own link-layer address. When a binding is first created, it MUST send a gratuitous ARP broadcast so neighbors update their caches.

Broadcasts reach a mobile node only if it set the B bit. A node can join multicast groups either through a local multicast router or through a bi-directional tunnel to its home agent. A mobile node can also be a router, responsible for whole networks that move together, such as on a ship or a train.
sections.eli5: Letters for you still go to your old house. Your parents catch them there, put each in a bigger envelope and mail it to your new address, where it is opened and given to you.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Registration redirects a node's traffic, which would be a serious vulnerability if it were not authenticated. ARP is also unauthenticated, and gratuitous ARP brings all of its risks. Home agents and mobile nodes MUST be able to authenticate, with keyed MD5 and a 128-bit key by default. Foreign agents MUST also support keyed MD5 with manual key distribution. Messages involving foreign agents are not all required to be authenticated, because key distribution is hard without a key management protocol.

The Identification field protects against replay. Timestamp-based protection is mandatory: the 64-bit value follows NTP format and MUST exceed all earlier accepted values. Nonce-based protection is optional, and the RFC points to a patent that may apply to it. If a timestamp is rejected, the home agent replies with code 133 and supplies its own time so the node can resynchronize.

The RFC does not provide confidentiality. Users with sensitive data should use encryption outside this document, and a node wanting location privacy can tunnel its traffic back through its home agent.
sections.eli5: Without a secret password, a stranger could call your parents and say "send all of this person's mail to me". The password and a fresh number in each call stop that.
